summary: Explains that the Tao of the IETF, previously published as a series of RFCs, is instead to be published as a web page. It also sets out the procedure for publishing and editing that page. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 9592.

plainLanguage.summary: A guidebook for newcomers used to be printed again and again. This memo says to keep it on a website that can be fixed anytime, and explains who may fix it.

questions: where is the tao of the ietf published
how is the tao of the ietf edited
why is the tao a web page
subtitle: Moving the Tao of the IETF from RFCs to a live web page

tldr.problem: The Tao of the IETF, a guide to how the IETF works, was published as an RFC which made it difficult to update when the content changed.
tldr.mechanism: The Tao is now maintained as a web page at ietf.org/tao.html, with an editor chosen by the IESG, changes discussed on a mailing list, and new versions archived with timestamps.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 9592, which updated the procedures.

today: RFC 6722 was obsoleted by RFC 9592, which updated the procedures for maintaining the Tao web page.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Tao of the IETF is an informal guide explaining how IETF meetings work, how Working Groups operate, the structure of related organizations, and an overview of the standards process. For many years it was published as an RFC, appearing in RFCs 1391, 1539, 1718, 3160, and most recently 4677.

RFC 6722 announces that the Tao will no longer be published as RFCs but instead as a web page that can be updated frequently without waiting for RFC Editor cycles. It also formally obsoletes RFC 4677, replacing it with the web version.
sections.plainLanguage: A book that explains how the IETF works used to get reprinted as a brand new document every time it changed. Now it lives on a website where updates happen instantly.

sections.title: Publishing and Editing Procedures
sections.content:
The Tao is published at ietf.org/tao.html in both HTTP and HTTPS versions. An editor or editors are designated by the IESG to maintain the page. Changes are proposed and discussed on the tao-discuss@ietf.org mailing list.

The process for accepting changes is deliberate: the editor prepares proposed revisions and publishes them at tao-possible-revision.html for IESG review. The IESG decides which changes to accept, then the IETF Secretariat publishes the approved version. All published versions are archived with timestamps in the format tao-YYYYMMDD.html, allowing readers to see what the Tao said at any point in history.
sections.plainLanguage: People suggest changes on a mailing list, the editor puts together the ideas, the leaders vote on them, then they go live on the website. Every old version is saved with a date stamp.

sections.title: Earlier Proposals
sections.content:
Before the decision to use a web page with IESG oversight, many alternative approaches were discussed. Some wanted just a simple web page. Others wanted periodic snapshots frozen as RFCs for formal record. Some proposed a wiki where any IETF participant could edit, with a master editor to revert bad changes. Others suggested a wiki with restricted edit permissions.

The procedure adopted was the rough consensus outcome of these discussions: a web page with centralized editor and IESG oversight, balancing the desire for frequent updates against the need for controlled quality and consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: People had lots of ideas: maybe a wiki, maybe new RFC documents every few months, maybe something simpler. They picked a system that lets it change quickly but still keeps the IETF leaders in control.

references.text: Hoffman, P. and S. Harris, "The Tao of IETF - A Novice's Guide to the Internet Engineering Task Force", BCP 17, RFC 4677, September 2006.
